content: Individuals who have experienced rheumatic fever in the past are at a significantly elevated risk of experiencing recurrent episodes of rheumatic fever and developing rheumatic heart disease, particularly following a streptococcal throat infection. Administering penicillin to these individuals has been shown to prevent both recurrent rheumatic fever and the subsequent development of rheumatic heart disease. However, there is no consensus regarding the optimal method of penicillin administration for this purpose. The objective of this analysis was to evaluate the effects of penicillin compared to a placebo, as well as to compare the efficacy of different penicillin regimens and formulations in preventing streptococcal infections and recurrent rheumatic fever. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACs, covering studies published up to June 2009. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed, and experts in the field were consulted. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized and quasi-randomized studies that compared (i) penicillin with a control group, (ii) oral penicillin with intramuscular penicillin, and (iii) different intramuscular penicillin regimens, such as 2or 3-weekly versus 4-weekly injections, in patients with a history of rheumatic fever. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted the relevant data. A total of nine studies involving 3008 participants were included in the analysis. Due to significant heterogeneity among the studies, the data were not pooled. Overall, the methodological quality of the included studies was deemed poor. Three trials, involving 1301 participants, compared penicillin with a control group. Of these, only one study demonstrated that penicillin significantly reduced the recurrence of rheumatic fever (relative risk [RR] 0.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.22 to 0.92) and streptococcal throat infections (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.97). Four trials, involving 1098 participants, compared intramuscular penicillin with oral penicillin. All four studies consistently showed that intramuscular penicillin was more effective than oral penicillin in reducing both rheumatic fever recurrence and streptococcal throat infections. One trial, involving 360 participants, compared 2-weekly with 4-weekly intramuscular penicillin injections. The results indicated that 2-weekly injections were superior in reducing the recurrence of rheumatic fever (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.83) and streptococcal throat infections (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.85). Another trial, involving 249 participants, compared 3-weekly with 4-weekly intramuscular penicillin injections. This study found that 3-weekly injections were more effective in reducing streptococcal throat infections (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.92) compared to 4-weekly injections. In conclusion, intramuscular penicillin appears to be more effective than oral penicillin in preventing the recurrence of rheumatic fever and streptococcal throat infections. Furthermore, more frequent intramuscular injections, such as 2-weekly or 3-weekly regimens, seem to be more effective than 4-weekly injections. However, it is important to note that these findings are based on studies of poor methodological quality, which limits the strength of the evidence.
